historical_timeline.summary: A generalized tonic-clonic seizure is documented in one account; the timing of onset is disputed.
Diagnosed with epilepsy shortly before he was taken to the prison at Omsk, by one account.
Debilitated by epilepsy, which worsened during his four years of forced labor.
Sought expert advice abroad from Romberg and Trousseau; began playing roulette on the same tour of Europe.
Gambled away his travel funds at Wiesbaden and was stranded there for about two months.
Wrote that his gambling was over; never returned to the roulette table.

claims.statement: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was born in Moscow on 11 November 1821 and died in St. Petersburg on 9 February 1881.
Dostoevsky had epilepsy throughout his literary career; in 1863 he went abroad to seek expert advice from the neurologists Romberg and Trousseau.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the modern epilepsy problem.

claims.statement: Accounts of when his epilepsy began and was diagnosed differ. One account places seizures in his student years (1838 to 1843), a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in 1844, and a diagnosis of epilepsy in 1849, shortly before he was taken to the prison at Omsk; another says the first symptoms appeared in early adulthood and the diagnosis came about a decade later; a third calls the onset controversial.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The timing of onset and diagnosis is unresolved; the record says only that seizures began in early adulthood.

claims.statement: He was sentenced to four years of forced labor at the Siberian prison in Omsk; his seizures worsened during his imprisonment, and by 1853 he was quite debilitated by epilepsy.
He described lack of sleep, alcohol, and overwork as triggers of his seizures, and he felt that the illness had damaged his memory.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports the modern counseling about seizure triggers and the attention to memory after seizures.

claims.statement: The type of his epilepsy is disputed: it has been interpreted as temporolimbic epilepsy, as an idiopathic generalized epilepsy with minor temporal involvement, as a cryptogenic focal epilepsy of frontomedial or temporal origin, and, for the ecstatic onset he described, as insular in origin.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; no seizure type or epilepsy syndrome is coded from it.

claims.statement: Whether the ecstatic experience he described before some seizures, and gave to characters in his fiction, was an epileptic aura is disputed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Not used in the modern seizure description.

claims.statement: He portrayed up to six characters with epilepsy in his fiction, from Murin in The Landlady (1847) to Smerdyakov in The Brothers Karamazov (1880).

His passion for roulette began on a tour of Europe in 1863. He fell into a pattern of chasing his losses and often pawned belongings so that he could gamble further. He gambled at Wiesbaden, Baden-Baden, and Bad Homburg, and the compulsion caused repeated financial trouble for about ten years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the modern gambling disorder.

claims.statement: In August 1865 he gambled away his travel funds at Wiesbaden and was stranded there for about two months, until he obtained money to leave.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Falls in the true frame of this episode, after the index date; anchors the synthetic lapse at the eight-month visit.

claims.statement: After returning to Russia he wrote the novella The Gambler, set in a fictional spa town called Roulettenburg, in 26 days.

In a letter of April 1871 he wrote that he had rid himself of "the abominable delusion that has tormented me for almost 10 years" and that "this was the very last time"; he never returned to the roulette table.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of stopping; it falls after the episode's true frame.

claims.statement: One retrospective review links his gambling to his epilepsy: the stress of gambling, together with sleep deprivation, is described as aggravating his seizures.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports the modern counseling that sleep loss at the tables is a seizure trigger.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary-care and neurology management of long-untreated epilepsy in a 43-year-old man (ILAE classification when the onset cannot be determined, routine and sleep-deprived EEG, epilepsy-protocol MRI, antiseizure medicine choice with slow lamotrigine titration and rash teaching, a seizure diary, trigger management, seizure safety and driving counseling, SUDEP discussion, bone health, and mood screening because depression is common in epilepsy) together with gambling-disorder care (a validated screen, cognitive behavioral therapy, self-exclusion, financial safeguards, peer support, and structured suicide-risk assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), including an honest account of a breakthrough seizure and a gambling lapse, on the AAN/AES and ILAE guidance, the CMID depression monograph, and current gambling-disorder evidence.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Dostoevsky is a 43-year-old man with recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures, untreated for many years, and gambling disorder, who returns four weeks after his first visit and is seen by neurology today. He has had one seizure since then, about three weeks ago, at home in the early morning after writing through the night; he lives alone and woke on the floor with a bitten tongue, aching muscles, and several hours of confusion. He recalls no warning. The routine EEG two weeks ago and the epilepsy-protocol MRI were both normal. He has not gambled since the first visit. He has signed up for self-exclusion from the casinos in the state and from licensed online sites, his bank has placed a gambling block on his cards, and he has started weekly cognitive behavioral therapy with a gambling-disorder therapist. Urges are strong in the evenings, especially when money is short. A friend he trusts now co-signs any withdrawal over a set amount. He has no thoughts of suicide. He is not driving.

assessment_plan.assessment: Neurology confirms epilepsy: many unprovoked seizures over years. With no clear onset and a normal EEG and MRI, the seizures are classified as generalized tonic-clonic seizures of unknown onset and the epilepsy as of unknown type, with unknown cause. Treatment is clearly indicated. After discussion of valproate, levetiracetam, and lamotrigine, he chose lamotrigine, which suits an epilepsy of unknown type, does not lower mood, and does not affect bone metabolism

hpi.narrative: Mr. Dostoevsky returns nine weeks after starting lamotrigine; he has taken 100 mg twice daily for three weeks. He had one generalized seizure in the third week of the titration, while on 50 mg a day, after a night without sleep to finish a manuscript; a friend who was with him timed it at about two minutes and followed the seizure action plan. He has had none since reaching 150 mg a day. He has had no rash, mouth sores, or fever, and no dizziness or double vision. The sleep-deprived EEG six weeks ago was normal. He has not gambled. He has attended every weekly therapy session and is learning to spot the thoughts that lead him to chase losses. He went to two Gamblers Anonymous meetings and saw the debt counselor, who is drawing up a repayment plan. His mood is better. He has no thoughts of suicide.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Dostoevsky returns three weeks after coming home from two months abroad. About four weeks ago, in a spa town he had not planned to visit, he went into a casino and played roulette on four evenings over one week, losing about two months of his income; he borrowed money to come home. On the second of those nights he stayed at the tables until morning and missed his evening lamotrigine dose, then missed it again the next evening. The following morning he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in his hotel room, witnessed by a member of staff, lasting about two minutes; he bit his tongue and was confused for some hours. He was checked in a local emergency department and released the same day; he brought the discharge letter, which records a normal examination and no injury. He has taken every dose since and has had no further seizure. He did not tell the clinic until today, because he felt ashamed. He had arranged no telehealth therapy sessions before leaving and had none while away. He has not gambled since he came home three weeks ago. He feels ashamed and worried about the new debt but says he has no thoughts of suicide and wants to get back on track.

He has been sipping an oral rehydration drink since last night and has kept it down. He slept poorly with the illness and is worried that the missed doses and the lost sleep will bring on a seizure. He has not gambled.

assessment.assessment: Epilepsy is confirmed by many unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart; a normal EEG and MRI do not exclude it. Under the ILAE classification the seizures are generalized tonic-clonic seizures of unknown onset and the epilepsy is of unknown type, with unknown cause, because neither the history nor the tests show whether the seizures begin focally or in both hemispheres. A sleep-deprived EEG may still clarify this. Treatment is clearly indicated, because the recurrence risk is high and every generalized tonic-clonic seizure carries a risk of injury and of SUDEP

For an epilepsy of unknown type the medicine should work for both focal and generalized seizures. Valproate is the most effective for generalized and unclassified epilepsy, but it causes weight gain, tremor, and liver and metabolic effects. Levetiracetam starts quickly but can cause irritability and low mood, a concern with his depressive symptoms and gambling. Lamotrigine is effective and well tolerated, has mood-stabilizing effects, and is not an enzyme inducer, but it must be increased slowly to lower the risk of a serious rash. After discussion he chose lamotrigine
Living alone, sleeping irregularly, and having uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures, some at night, are the main SUDEP risk factors. Good seizure control lowers the risk most

assessment.display: Gambling disorder and mood in relation to his epilepsy
assessment.assessment: Nights at the tables mean lost sleep and missed doses, so his gambling and his seizures share triggers. Depression and anxiety are common in epilepsy, and all antiseizure medicines carry a warning about suicidal thoughts, which matters more because gambling disorder raises suicide risk. Lamotrigine has no interaction with the treatments planned for his gambling

recommendations: Start lamotrigine today: 25 mg daily for two weeks, 50 mg daily for two weeks, 50 mg twice daily for one week, 75 mg twice daily for one week, then 100 mg twice daily; primary care to check for rash at each dose step
Stop lamotrigine and seek care the same day for any rash, mouth sores, fever, or swollen glands
Sleep-deprived EEG in about three weeks

A lamotrigine trough level once at steady state as his reference, and again only after a breakthrough seizure, if nonadherence is suspected, or when an interacting medicine is started; no routine blood count or liver tests on lamotrigine
No rescue medicine now, because his seizures are single and brief; review if they become prolonged or come in clusters
Bone health: vitamin D is adequate and lamotrigine is not an enzyme inducer, so no DXA scan
A seizure diary, regular sleep with no writing through the night, little alcohol, and pill organizer and phone alarms for adherence
No driving until he has been seizure-free for a sustained period and I have reviewed him; showers rather than baths, no swimming or climbing alone, and care with stoves and sharp tools
SUDEP discussed today; a written seizure action plan for friends, who should call 911 for a seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures, injury, or seizures in water
PHQ-9 and a suicide-risk review in primary care at each visit; continue gambling-disorder treatment
Neurology review in about ten months, in January, or sooner after any breakthrough seizure; primary care manages the titration and monitoring in between
